url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide.md

# Getting Started

`@deltabox/toolchain` is an all-in-one project toolchain. You drop a
`dbx.config.ts` at a repo root and the toolchain generates and manages
your configs, tsconfigs, changelogs, CI and more — from the CLI, the programmatic
API and the VS Code extension.

## Install

```bash
# as a dev dependency in the project you want to manage
yarn add -D @deltabox/toolchain

# or for global usage
npm install -g @deltabox/toolchain
```

The published package exposes one binary, `dbx`:

```bash
yarn dbx --help
```

## Create a config

Scaffold a config for a project that does not have one yet:

```bash
dbx project:config        # detect + write dbx.config.ts
```

Or start from a template:

```bash
dbx template:list
dbx create --template project --name my-app --out ./my-app
```

## Sync

`sync` runs every enabled task and writes the managed files (adding a manifest at
`.dbx/toolchain/manifest.json`):

```bash
dbx sync              # write managed files
dbx sync --check      # CI: fail if files are out of date
dbx sync --recursive  # every discovered project, in dependency order
dbx watch             # re-sync on change
```

The generated state lives under `.dbx/`. Add it to `.gitignore`, keeping only
the manifest (it holds no absolute paths):

```gitignore
.dbx/*
!.dbx/toolchain
.dbx/toolchain/*
!.dbx/toolchain/manifest.json
```

`dbx sync` adds this block to an existing `.gitignore` automatically, so you only
need to add it by hand when the repo has no `.gitignore` yet.

## What gets managed

| Area                                                                | Section in the config |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| GitHub workflows, commitlint, Conventional-Commits VS Code settings | `changelog`           |
| `biome.json` (Biome consumers)                                      | `biome`               |
| Workspace `tsconfig.json` files (aliases + references)              | `tsconfig`            |
| `vite.config.ts` (Vite+ consumers)                                  | `vite`                |
| Template sources / scaffolding                                      | `templates`           |
| Package catalogs (`.yarnrc.yml` / `pnpm-workspace.yaml`)            | `catalogs`            |
| Watch behaviour                                                     | `watch`               |

Every section is **opt-in by presence**: define it to enable it, omit it to leave
that area untouched.

# Monorepo Guide

## Project graph

`dbx projects` discovers every workspace package and writes a
dependency graph to `.dbx/toolchain/projects.json`. The VS Code extension and the
`sync --recursive` command consume it.

## tsconfig generation

Enable the `tsconfig` section and the toolchain generates each workspace's
`tsconfig.json` (extending `tsconfig.default.json`) and, for a monorepo root, a
`tsconfig.workspaces.json` wiring project references and path aliases:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: { type: 'monorepo-root', name: 'acme', scope: '@acme' },
        tsconfig: { refs: true, aliases: true, indent: 4 },
    },
});
```

See the [tsconfig guide](/guide/tsconfig) for every option and why the toolchain
splits the config across several files.

## Scaffolding a monorepo

```bash
dbx project:init:monorepo --name acme --scope @acme --out .
dbx project:init:workspace --name utils --scope @acme --root . --dir packages/utils
```

## Tasks

This repo (and Vite+ consumers) use **Vite Task** (`dbx run`) instead of Turbo.
The package graph orders execution via each package's `package.json`
dependencies.

Each package declares `build`, `typecheck` and `test` in its own
`vite.config.ts` with explicit cache input/output, so `dbx run` reports cache
hits (a `package.json` script cannot carry cache config):

```ts
// packages/<pkg>/vite.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
    run: {
        tasks: {
            build: {
                command: 'tsdown --config-loader unrun',
                cache: {
                    input: [{ auto: true }, '!dist/**', '!**/*.tsbuildinfo'],
                    output: ['dist/**'],
                },
            },
            typecheck: {
                command: 'tsc -p tsconfig.build.json --noEmit',
                cache: { input: [{ auto: true }, '!**/*.tsbuildinfo'], output: [] },
            },
            test: {
                command: 'vitest run',
                cache: { input: [{ auto: true }, '!**/*.tsbuildinfo'], output: [] },
            },
        },
    },
});
```

The root `package.json` orchestrates them and adds the umbrella build:

```json
{
    "scripts": {
        "build": "dbx run --filter \"./packages/*\" build && dbx run build:root",
        "test": "dbx run --filter \"./packages/*\" test && dbx run test:root"
    }
}
```

`dbx run --filter "./packages/*" build` runs each package's `build` in
dependency order (excluding the root, which avoids recursion), then `build:root`
builds the umbrella dist.

# VS Code Extension

The `deltabox toolchain` extension provides a sidebar for managing projects.

## Install

Download from the [Visual Studio Code Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=deltabox.toolchain-vscode).

or through the CLI:

```bash
code --install-extension deltabox.toolchain-vscode
```

## Commands

| Command                      | What it does                                                                            |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Sync all / active / selected | Run `dbx sync` (`--recursive` / per project).                                           |
| Check sync                   | `sync --check` across the workspace.                                                    |
| Scaffold project             | Single project, monorepo root (with/without example), workspace, or **From template…**. |
| Add template…                | `template:init --add` on a folder you pick (any kind).                                  |
| Remove template…             | `template:list --registry` then `template:remove`.                                      |
| Generate configs             | `project:config` for projects missing a config.                                         |
| Run workflow                 | Trigger generated GitHub workflows.                                                     |
| Run Vite+ command…           | QuickPick over the Vite+ provider commands, run in a terminal.                          |
| Create Vite+ project…        | `vp create` in a terminal.                                                              |
| Add provider...              | Register a custom provider in `.dbx/toolchain/providers.json`.                          |
| Run command...               | Run a provider command (`dbx <command>`) in a terminal.                                 |
| Create from template...      | `dbx create --template <id>` (terminal for online templates).                           |
| Reset tooling                | Remove generated files / manifest / config.                                             |
| Toggle auto-sync             | Enable/disable sync-on-change.                                                          |

Interactive commands (the dev server, `vp create`, online scaffolding) run in an
integrated terminal at the project root; everything else runs in the output
channel.

## Project menu

Every project card (and every project in the **Projects** tree) exposes the same
actions, scoped to that project:

* **Sync** / **Check sync** — regenerate / verify the project's managed files.
* **Generate config** — write a `dbx.config.ts`.
* **Run workflow…** — trigger one of the project's generated GitHub workflows.
* **Run Vite+ command…** — run a `vp` command in that project.
* **Reset tooling…** — remove the generated files + manifest, or everything
  including the config.
* **Go to project** — reveal the project in the Explorer.

## Providers, templates and Vite+ in the editor

The **Providers** and **Templates** views read `dbx providers --json` and `dbx template:list --json`, so adding one surfaces it in the UI automatically.

**Add provider...** writes a custom provider to `.dbx/toolchain/providers.json`, which `toolchainProviders()` merges with the built-ins, so a registered provider's commands also become `dbx` commands (`dbx <command>`), runnable from the view.

**Add template...** runs `template:init --add`.

**Remove template source...** runs `template:list --registry` + `template:remove`.

**Create from template…** prompts for the template's inputs and actions (see
[Templates](/guide/templates)) before running `dbx create`. Scaffolding also asks
for a package manager (`yarn` default).

The Home view links to this documentation with **Need help? Go to documentation**.

## Auto-sync

Auto-sync watches input files only: `dbx.config.*`, `tsconfig.default.json`, and `tsconfig.workspaces.json`.

Generated outputs are never watched. The scheduler debounces bursts, allows one sync at a time, queues at most one follow-up, and suppresses events briefly after a run.

When a sync finds no workspace tsconfig files while `tsconfig.refs`/`tsconfig.composite` are on (or a `tsconfig.workspaces.json` is present), the extension surfaces the CLI's warning as a notification (once per session) with a **Show output** action.

## Settings

| Setting                       | Default                 | Description                   |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------- |
| `deltabox.toolchain.enabled`  | `true`                  | Auto sync on watched changes. |
| `deltabox.toolchain.debounce` | `300`                   | Debounce (ms) before a sync.  |
| `deltabox.toolchain.command`  | `sync`                  | The command to run on change. |
| `deltabox.toolchain.watch`    | config + tsconfig globs | Inputs that trigger a sync.   |

## Command palette

Search for `deltabox:` to find:

* **Sync active project**
* **Sync selected projects**
* **Sync all projects**
* **Check sync**
* **Scaffold project…**
* **Add template…**
* **Remove template…**
* **Add provider...**
* **Refresh providers**
* **Add template...**
* **Remove template source...**
* **Refresh templates**
* **Generate configs…**
* **Run workflow…**
* **Run Vite+ command…**
* **Create Vite+ project…**
* **Reset tooling…**
* **Refresh projects**
* **Toggle auto-sync**

# LLMs

This documentation is published in machine-readable forms so LLMs and coding
agents can read it efficiently, following the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org)
standard:

* [`/llms.txt`](/llms.txt) — a concise, link-first overview: a short description,
  how the toolchain works, and a table of contents linking to the Markdown
  version of every page. Small enough to fit in a context window.
* [`/llms-full.txt`](/llms-full.txt) — the **entire** documentation concatenated
  into a single Markdown file, for when an agent wants everything in one fetch.

Every page is also available as raw Markdown by appending `.md` to its URL (eg.
`/guide/tsconfig.md`).

## When the site is unavailable

If `https://toolchain.deltabox.studio` is down, the same documentation lives in
the repository at
[github.com/deltabox-studio/toolchain/tree/main/apps/docs](https://github.com/deltabox-studio/toolchain/tree/main/apps/docs).

# CLI

The `dbx` binary is composed from framework-agnostic command
descriptors. Commands that run against a project load its
`dbx.config.ts` first, so config-derived defaults apply unless you
override them on the command line.

## Global flags

| Flag                | Description                                                    |
| ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--log-level <lvl>` | Minimum log level: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `silent`. |
| `--color`           | Force coloured output (the default).                           |
| `--no-color`        | Disable coloured output.                                       |
| `--no-update-check` | Do not check for a newer `dbx` version.                        |

These override the [`logger` config](/guide/config#logging) and may appear
before or after the subcommand.

`dbx` checks the npm registry in the background (about once a day) and prints a
short notice with a link to the release when a newer version is published. The
check is skipped in CI and when `NO_UPDATE_NOTIFIER` or `DBX_NO_UPDATE_CHECK` is
set, and can be turned off with `--no-update-check`.

## Output

Colour is on by default and follows `--no-color` / the [`logger` config](/guide/config#logging).

## Core

| Command     | Description                                                                      |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `projects`  | Discover projects and write `.dbx/toolchain/projects.json`.                      |
| `sync`      | Regenerate every managed file (`--check`, `--recursive`, `--watch`, `--force`).  |
| `watch`     | Sync once, then watch key inputs and re-sync.                                    |
| `reset`     | Remove generated files, the manifest and/or the config (`--all`, `--recursive`). |
| `providers` | List registered providers + their commands (`--json`).                           |

## Scaffolding

| Command                  | Description                                                                     |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `project:init`           | A single-package TypeScript project (`--package-manager`).                      |
| `project:init:monorepo`  | A monorepo root (add `--example` for one example workspace).                    |
| `project:init:workspace` | A workspace package into an existing monorepo root.                             |
| `project:config`         | Generate `dbx.config.ts` for projects missing one.                              |
| `create`                 | Scaffold from a template (`--template`/`--kind`, `--name`, `--scope`, `--out`). |

Templates that declare inputs/actions are prompted for them (`--var key=value`,
`--action <id>`), see [Templates](/guide/templates).

On an interactive terminal, a bare `dbx create` (no `--template`/`--kind`/`--name`)
prompts for the template, name and scope with clack; Ctrl-C cancels. See
[Templates](/guide/templates).

## Templates

| Command           | Description                                                            |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `template:list`   | List templates (`--kind`, `--registry`, `--online`, `--json`).         |
| `template:init`   | Write a `template.json` to a directory (`--kind`, `--name`, `--add`).  |
| `template:add`    | Record a source in `.dbx/toolchain/templates.json` (auto-inits local). |
| `template:remove` | Remove a source by id or `type:locate`.                                |
| `template:info`   | Show one template.                                                     |

See [Templates](/guide/templates).

## Migrations

```bash
dbx migrate --from biome --write           # .oxfmtrc.json + .oxlintrc.json
dbx migrate --from biome --target vite --write
dbx migrate --from all                     # every detected source
dbx migrate --from vite --recursive --write  # migrate every detected project
dbx migrate --check                        # CI: exit 1 when stale
dbx migrate:list
```

See [Migrations](/guide/migrations).

## Tsconfig / cleanup / changelog / workflows

| Command                     | Description                                               |
| --------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tsconfig`                  | Regenerate workspace `tsconfig.json` files.               |
| `cleanup` / `cleanup:turbo` | Remove build artifacts / the turbo cache.                 |
| `changelog`                 | Derive the semver bump and update CHANGELOG + versions.   |
| `workflow`                  | Trigger generated GitHub workflows via `gh workflow run`. |

## Providers

Every provider subcommand is a passthrough. Vite+ commands are reachable both
directly and through the `vite` namespace:

```bash
dbx fmt                 # a bare Vite+ command forwards to `vp fmt`
dbx run -r build        # forwards to `vp run -r build`
dbx vite dev            # explicit namespace (always works)
dbx vite:build          # named alias for `vp build`
```

A bare `dbx <command>` is forwarded to Vite+ when the name (or a Vite+ alias)
matches — built-in commands win, so `dbx migrate` stays the toolchain's
migration. The `vite` command forwards its operands verbatim, so **every** Vite+
CLI command and flag is reachable.

## Programmatic

The CLI is assembled from framework-agnostic command descriptors, so a consumer
can build its own program (or reuse the routing helpers):

```ts
import {
    createCli,
    runCli,
    builtinCommands,
    registerToolchainCommands,
    withDefaultVite,
    extractLogOptions,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/cli';
```

| Export                                         | Description                                                            |
| ---------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `createCli()`                                  | Build the `dbx` commander program (global flags + built-in commands).  |
| `runCli(argv?)`                                | Parse and run the CLI (extracts logger flags, then defaults Vite+).    |
| `builtinCommands()`                            | The commands built into the root CLI (config commands need an engine). |
| `registerToolchainCommands(program, commands)` | Wire `ToolchainCommand[]` descriptors onto a commander program.        |
| `withDefaultVite(argv, commandNames?)`         | Insert `vite` before a bare Vite+ command (built-ins win).             |
| `extractLogOptions(argv)`                      | Pull `--log-level` / `--color` / `--no-color` out of argv.             |

`extractLogOptions` makes the logger flags work before *or* after the
subcommand and stops at `--`, so a wrapped binary's own flags are never eaten.
`withDefaultVite` powers the bare-command passthrough described above:

```ts
extractLogOptions(['node', 'dbx', 'sync', '--no-color']);
// { argv: ['node', 'dbx', 'sync'], options: { color: false } }

withDefaultVite(['node', 'dbx', 'fmt', '--check']);
// ['node', 'dbx', 'vite', 'fmt', '--check']
```

## Config generator

The generic Zod/env config engine is not a `dbx` command: a consumer
builds an engine with `createConfigEngine` and registers the `config:*` commands
on its **own** CLI. See [Config Generator](/guide/config-generator).

---

url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/config.md

# Configuration

A project is driven by a single `dbx.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: {
            type: 'monorepo-root',
            name: 'acme',
            scope: '@acme',
        },
        changelog: {
            workflows: { ci: true, release: true },
            branches: { main: 'main', dev: 'dev' },
        },
        tsconfig: { refs: true },
        biome: true,
        vite: {
            fmt: { semi: true, singleQuote: true },
            lint: { ignorePatterns: ['dist/**'] },
            test: { include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'] },
        },
        watch: { debounce: 150 },
    },
});
```

The `@deltabox/toolchain` settings live under the `toolchain` key, so a
`dbx.config.ts` can host other dbx concerns alongside it.

Each section has its own guide: [Project](/guide/project),
[Changelog](/guide/changelog), [tsconfig](/guide/tsconfig), [Biome](/guide/biome),
[Vite+](/guide/vite), [Watch](/guide/watch), [Logger](/guide/logger) and
[Providers](/guide/providers).

## Opt-in by presence

Every section under `toolchain` is **opt-in by presence**: the toolchain only
touches an area you actually ask for.

* Omit a section — that area is left completely alone.
* `section: true` — enable it with defaults.
* `section: false` — explicitly disable it.
* `section: { ...options }` — enable and configure it.

Helpers `sectionEnabled(section)` and `sectionConfig(section)` implement this and
are exported for programmatic use.

## Nested configs

A `dbx.config.*` in a **non-root** folder (a workspace, an app, a nested
project) is merged over the nearest ancestor `dbx.config.*` found while walking
up to the repository root (the walk stops at the `.git` boundary, so it never
picks up a config from outside the repo).

The merge is recursive:

* **Objects** are merged key by key, so a child keeps every option it does not
  mention.
* **Leaves** — booleans, strings, numbers and **arrays** — in the child
  **replace** the root's value (arrays are not concatenated).

This makes a shared root config plus small per-project overrides possible:

```ts
// <root>/dbx.config.ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        changelog: { scopes: ['core', 'cli'], branches: { main: 'main', dev: 'dev' } },
        tsconfig: { refs: true, aliases: true },
    },
});

// <root>/packages/web/dbx.config.ts — inherits changelog + tsconfig, tweaks both
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        changelog: { scopes: ['web'] }, // replaces the root's `scopes` array
        tsconfig: { refs: false }, // boolean overrides the root's `refs`
    },
});
```

The workspace above ends up with `changelog.branches` from the root (unchanged),
`changelog.scopes: ['web']` (replaced), and `tsconfig: { refs: false, aliases: true }`.

> **`project` is inherited except its identity fields.** `name`, `scope`,
> `description` and `type` are per-project, so a non-root config keeps its own (or
> falls back to its `package.json`) and is still detected from its own files — a
> root `project` never renames a workspace. The shared fields (`author`,
> `license`, `homepage`, `repo`, `packageManager`, ...) flow down so their
> `package.json` values and replacement tokens stay shared.
> `project: { inherit: false }` disables project inheritance entirely. `hooks`
> are not inherited either — a parent's hooks are code and do not run for a
> nested project's sync.

## `defineConfig`

`defineConfig` is an identity helper that gives the file full type-checking and
autocomplete (it mirrors Vite's `defineConfig`).

## Config file names

The loader looks for, in order:

```
dbx.config.ts
dbx.config.mts
dbx.config.js
dbx.config.mjs
dbx.config.cjs
dbx.config.json
```

## Hooks

`.ts`/`.js` configs can declare lifecycle hooks (JSON cannot):

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        hooks: {
            afterLoad: ({ tokens }) => console.log(tokens),
            beforeSync: ctx => ctx.log('syncing…'),
            afterTask: ({ task, files }) => console.log(task.name, files?.length),
            afterSync: ({ result }) => console.log(result.written.length),
            onChange: ({ path }) => console.log('changed', path),
        },
    },
});
```

Return values are awaited.

## Logging

Every toolchain message goes through one logger. Configure it in the config:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        logger: { level: 'debug', color: false, name: 'dbx' },
    },
});
```

| Option  | Values                                             | Default |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------- |
| `level` | `debug` | `info` | `warn` | `error` | `silent` | `info`  |
| `color` | `true` | `false`                                  | `true`  |
| `name`  | prefix for non-indented lines                      | `dbx`   |

Colour is **on by default** (the toolchain forces it rather than relying on TTY
autodetection); `--no-color` or `logger: { color: false }` turn it off. Human
output is rendered with [`@clack/prompts`](https://bombshell.dev/clack) — level
symbols (`•` info, `◆` success, `▲` warn, `■` error) and a guide.

On the CLI, `--log-level <level>` and `--no-color` override the config (see the
[CLI reference](/guide/cli)). Machine output (`--json`) is written unprefixed
through the same logger.

## Providers

Provider passthrough commands (Vite+) follow the logger's colour setting. The
`providers` section can force provider colours on or off on its own:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        providers: { color: false },
    },
});
```

| Option  | Values            | Default        |
| ------- | ----------------- | -------------- |
| `color` | `true` | `false` | inherit logger |

`color: false` runs the wrapped binary with `NO_COLOR=1` and `FORCE_COLOR=0`, so
it emits plain output even on a colour terminal. The global CLI `--no-color`
flag turns provider colour off too. See [Providers](/guide/providers#colour).

## Vite+

The whole Vite+ config lives in `toolchain.vite`. Every key is passed through
verbatim to Vite+, so `dbx.config.*` stays the only hand-authored root config:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        vite: {
            test: { include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'], environment: 'node' },
            lint: { ignorePatterns: ['dist/**'] },
            fmt: { semi: true, singleQuote: true },
        },
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` writes a thin root `vite.config.ts` that resolves that config at load
time, so the generated file never duplicates (or drifts from) `dbx.config.*`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';

// Generated by @deltabox/toolchain — edit the vite section in dbx.config and run `dbx sync`.
import { resolveVite } from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';

export default defineConfig(resolveVite({ cwd: import.meta.dirname }));
```

`resolveVite(options?)` resolves the **same-directory** `dbx.config.*` (so a
nested `vite.config.ts` uses the nested config it sits next to), or the
`toolchain` you pass, then returns `toolchain.vite`. It is exported from
`@deltabox/toolchain/vite` for programmatic use too.

The single toolchain opt-out is `config`. Set `vite: { config: false }` to leave
a hand-written `vite.config.ts` alone. Everything else under `vite` is Vite+
config (plugins, `test`, `lint`, `fmt`, `run.tasks`, ...), so `toolchain.vite`
is the full Vite+ configuration. The section is typed as Vite+'s own config
(`ToolchainViteConfig` = Vite's `UserConfig` as augmented by Vite+), so the whole
Vite+ surface autocompletes in `dbx.config.ts`.

Add `/vite.config.ts` to `vite.fmt.ignorePatterns` so Oxfmt leaves the generated
shim alone — without it `vp fmt` would rewrite the shim and `dbx sync --check`
would report drift. `dbx migrate --from vite` adds it for you.

To adopt an existing hand-written `vite.config.ts`, fold it in with the
migration (see [Migrations](/guide/migrations#vite-config)):

```bash
dbx migrate --from vite --write   # folds the object into toolchain.vite (+ the fmt ignore)
dbx sync                          # writes the managed vite.config.ts shim
```

## Programmatic API

```ts
import { loadToolchainConfig, runSync, defaultSyncTasks } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

const { config, tokens, projectType } = await loadToolchainConfig(process.cwd());
await runSync({ tasks: defaultSyncTasks(), cwd: process.cwd(), config, tokens, projectType });
```

Full section reference: [dbx.config](/config/reference).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/project.md
---
# Project

The `project` section is a package's **canonical metadata**. It is the single
place to declare who a package is, and it does three jobs:

1. **Defines `package.json` fields.** On `dbx sync`, the fields the section
   defines are written into the project's `package.json` (everything else is left
   untouched).
2. **Feeds the `{{ token }}` replacements.** Every template (`biome.json`,
   workflows, tsconfigs, READMEs, ...) reads these values.
3. **Drives scaffolding.** `dbx project:init*` uses the section as its defaults
   (and `project.type` picks the kind of project to generate).

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: {
            type: 'monorepo-root',
            name: 'acme',
            scope: '@acme',
            author: 'Acme Inc. <hello@acme.dev>',
            license: 'MIT',
            homepage: 'https://acme.dev',
            repo: 'https://github.com/acme/acme',
            description: 'The acme monorepo',
            nodeVersion: '22',
            packageManager: 'yarn',
            packageManagerVersion: '4.17.1',
        },
    },
});
```

## `package.json` mapping

A sync writes only the fields the config **defines**; a field you omit is never
touched. The mapping:

| `project` field  | `package.json` field | Notes                                              |
| ---------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `name` + `scope` | `name`               | `@acme/app` when a scope is set, else `app`.       |
| `description`    | `description`        |                                                    |
| `author`         | `author`             |                                                    |
| `license`        | `license`            |                                                    |
| `homepage`       | `homepage`           |                                                    |
| `repo`           | `repository`         | `{ type: 'git', url }` (+ `directory`, see below). |
| `packageManager` | `packageManager`     | `yarn@4.17.1` when `packageManagerVersion` is set. |
| `type`           | —                    | Project kind for detection/scaffolding.            |
| `nodeVersion`    | —                    | Node version for CI/templates (not `engines`).     |

`nodeVersion` is intentionally **not** written to `engines`: it is the Node
version the generated workflows run on (`node-version: '{{nodeVersion}}'`), which
is a different concern from the published `engines.node` range.

## Workspace inheritance

A non-root `dbx.config.*` is merged over the nearest ancestor config (see
[Configuration → Nested configs](/guide/config#nested-configs)). For `project`
specifically:

* **Fields are inherited** (scope, author, license, ...), so a workspace keeps the
  shared metadata while overriding the fields it sets (typically `name`).
* **`type` is never inherited** — the project kind is location-specific, so a
  workspace without an explicit `type` is still detected from its own files.
* **`inherit: false`** opts out entirely: the project keeps only its own `project`
  and ignores the parent's (useful for an unrelated package inside the tree).

```ts
// packages/web/dbx.config.ts — keeps the root scope/author/license, sets its own name
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: { name: 'web' },
        // ...
    },
});
```

### `repo` resolves to the workspace path

For a non-root project, `repo` also resolves to the workspace's location in the
repository, written as `repository.directory`:

```json
{
    "repository": {
        "type": "git",
        "url": "https://github.com/acme/acme",
        "directory": "packages/web"
    }
}
```

The directory is computed relative to the repository root (the nearest ancestor
with a `.git`), exactly like npm expects for a monorepo workspace.

## When the section is absent

If `project` is not defined, nothing is written to `package.json` — and the
replacement tokens fall back to the project's **own `package.json`** values
(`name`/`scope` from `name`, plus `description`, `author`, `license`, `homepage`,
`repository`, `engines.node`, `packageManager`). So a repo with no `project`
section still generates correct tokens from its existing metadata.

## Scaffolding

`dbx project:init`, `dbx project:init:monorepo` and
`dbx project:init:workspace` read `project` as their defaults, and:

* **`name` is required** (from `--name` or `project.name`) — a scaffold fails
  with a clear error when it is missing.
* **`type` must be valid** (`project`, `monorepo-root` or `monorepo-workspace`)
  when passed explicitly or set in the config; an invalid value is rejected.

```bash
dbx project:init --name my-app --scope @acme --type project --out ./my-app
dbx project:init:monorepo --name acme --scope @acme --out .
dbx project:init:monorepo --name acme --scope @acme --example --out .
dbx project:init:workspace --name web --root . --dir packages/web
```

The scaffolded `dbx.config.ts` spells the resolved `project` fields out, so a
generated project is self-describing from day one.

Pass `--package-manager <pm>` (`yarn` default, or `pnpm` / `npm` / `bun`) to
choose the manager the scaffold targets.

## Package manager and catalogs

The scaffold and `dbx sync` write a **catalog** (`package -> version range`) into
the file the package manager reads it from, so dependencies can be declared with
`catalog:`:

| Manager | Catalog file          | Notes                                        |
| ------- | --------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `yarn`  | `.yarnrc.yml`         | `catalog:` / `catalogs:` (default + named).  |
| `pnpm`  | `pnpm-workspace.yaml` | `catalog:` / `catalogs:`.                    |
| `bun`   | `package.json`        | `workspaces.catalog`.                        |
| `npm`   | —                     | No catalog support; dependencies are pinned. |

Scaffolding resolves the manager from the `packageManager` input and writes the
catalog of the packages the project depends on. To keep it in sync with
`dbx sync`, add a `catalogs` section to `dbx.config.*`:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: { packageManager: 'yarn' },
        catalogs: {
            packages: { react: '^19.0.0', lodash: '^4.17.21' },
            named: { legacy: { react: '^18.0.0' } },
        },
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` writes (and keeps in sync) `catalog:` / `catalogs:` in `.yarnrc.yml`
(Yarn) or `pnpm-workspace.yaml` (pnpm). A catalog file is only written when it is
absent or already toolchain-managed (it carries a marker comment); a hand-written
one is left untouched. Bun catalogs live in `package.json` and npm has no catalog
support — both emit a warning.

## Programmatic API

```ts
import { projectFromPackageJson, projectToPackageJson, projectSyncTask } from '@deltabox/toolchain';

// Seed a config from an existing package.json.
const project = projectFromPackageJson(require('./package.json'));

// Map the defined fields onto package.json fields.
const pkgFields = projectToPackageJson(project, { directory: 'packages/web' });

// The sync task itself.
projectSyncTask();
```

| Export                        | Description                                                         |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `projectFromPackageJson(pkg)` | Derive project metadata from a `package.json`.                      |
| `projectToPackageJson(p, o?)` | Map defined project fields onto `package.json` fields.              |
| `projectSyncTask()`           | The sync task that applies the `project` section to `package.json`. |

url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/changelog.md
---
# Changelog & versioning

The `changelog` section drives everything Conventional Commits: the CI that
lints commit messages, the local husky hook, the `commitlint.config.mjs`, and the
changelog pipeline that bumps versions and writes `CHANGELOG.md`.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        changelog: {
            branches: { main: 'main', dev: 'dev' },
            workflows: { ci: true, changelog: true, release: true },
            types: ['feat', 'fix', 'docs', 'chore'],
            scopes: ['api', 'web', 'deps'],
            versioning: { target: 'individual', workspaces: ['packages/*', 'apps/*'] },
        },
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` writes the GitHub workflows (`.github/workflows`), the commitlint
config, and the husky `commit-msg` hook (`.husky/commit-msg`). Activate the hook
with a `postinstall` script (Yarn Berry never runs `prepare`):

```json
{ "scripts": { "commitlint": "commitlint", "postinstall": "husky" } }
```

See [Package scripts](/guide/scripts) for the full recommended script set.

## Workflows

`dbx sync` writes the GitHub workflows into `.github/workflows`. Each id (`ci`,
`changelog`, `release`, `issues`, `sync`) accepts one of three forms:

* `true` / `false` — write the generated default, or skip it;
* a **`WorkflowConfig` object** — override parts of the default (branches,
  triggers, extra top-level keys, extra steps/jobs, token overrides);
* a **raw YAML string** — written **verbatim** as the workflow file, for a
  workflow the object model can't express.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        changelog: {
            workflows: {
                ci: true, // the generated default
                issues: false, // don't write issues.yml
                release: { pushBranches: ['main'] }, // override the default
                // A fully hand-authored workflow, written as-is:
                sync: `name: Toolchain sync
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  sync:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: yarn dbx sync --check
`,
            },
        },
    },
});
```

A raw string is **not** merged with the default, is **not** token-replaced, and
gets **no generated header** — it is the file's exact content. The
`changelog.branches` defaults don't apply to it either (it defines its own
triggers). An empty string disables the workflow.

## Branches

`branches.main` and `branches.dev` pick which branches the generated workflows
target. Each accepts a glob or an array of globs:

| Branch | Drives                                                                         | Default              |
| ------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------- |
| `main` | The **CI** workflow (push), the **release** workflow, and the release PR base. | `['main']`           |
| `dev`  | The **changelog/version** workflow (push).                                     | none — reuses `main` |

`dev` has **no default**: when it is omitted the changelog workflow runs on
`main` (so a single-branch repo needs no `dev`). Set it for a `dev` → `main`
flow:

```ts
changelog: { branches: { main: 'main', dev: 'dev' } }
// or multiple branches per purpose:
changelog: { branches: { main: ['main', 'release/**'], dev: ['dev', 'next'] } }
```

The `sync` workflow runs on both. Any per-workflow `pushBranches` override (eg.
`workflows.ci.pushBranches`) still wins.

## commitlint config location

By default the generated `commitlint.config.mjs` lives at the project root. Set
`commitlint.dir` to write it elsewhere:

```ts
changelog: {
    commitlint: {
        dir: '.config';
    }
} // -> .config/commitlint.config.mjs
```

When a custom dir is set, the generated husky hook and the CI commitlint step
both pass `--config <dir>/commitlint.config.mjs`, so commitlint finds it. Note
that editor tooling that discovers the config by convention (eg. the
Conventional Commits VS Code extension, which loads from the repo root) expects
the config at the root — keep the default unless you have a reason to move it.

> The extension's `No "exports" main defined in … conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits …`
> error is an upstream commitlint bug (ESM-only parser preset), not a config
> discovery problem. See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

## Versioning

`versioning` controls whether — and where — a changelog run writes `version`
fields into `package.json`. It accepts a boolean or an object, and defaults to
`true`.

```ts
changelog: { versioning: true }                       // uniform, defaults
changelog: { versioning: false }                      // never write versions
changelog: { versioning: { target: 'root-only' } }
changelog: { versioning: { target: 'individual', workspaces: ['packages/*'] } }
```

### `target`

| Target       | What it bumps                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `uniform`    | The root (when it has a `package.json`) **and every workspace** to one shared version. **Default.**                                                                          |
| `root-only`  | Only the root `package.json`. Workspaces are left untouched and get no changelog entry.                                                                                      |
| `individual` | The root tracks the overall bump; **each workspace is bumped on its own** from the commits touching its files, so versions can drift apart (like an "independent" monorepo). |

With `versioning: false` no `version` field is written at all — the changelog
entries are still generated (headed as `uniform` would), so you can keep
versioning in another tool (for example changesets).

### `workspaces`

An array of glob patterns selecting the workspaces to version, relative to the
repo root. It resolves in this order:

1. the `workspaces` patterns you pass, when you pass them;
2. otherwise the root `package.json` `workspaces` field, when present;
3. otherwise the root `package.json` alone (a single-package repo);
4. otherwise a warning is logged and nothing is versioned.

```ts
changelog: { versioning: { target: 'individual', workspaces: ['packages/*', '!packages/private-*'] } }
```

`individual` uses a `git log` path filter per workspace, so a workspace is only
bumped when the scanned commit range touched a file inside it — or a file in one
of the workspaces it depends on (see [Workspace changelogs](#workspace-changelogs)).
The root's version always follows the overall bump derived from every scanned
commit.

### How a run decides its versions

Each run:

1. reads the commits in the range (`--range`/`--processing-method`, default
   `HEAD`);
2. derives the semver bump (`feat` → minor, `fix`/other → patch, `!` or a
   `BREAKING CHANGE` footer → major);
3. plans the versions per `target` + `workspaces` (see above);
4. writes the plan's `package.json` versions and prepends the new entry to the
   root `CHANGELOG.md` and each versioned workspace's `CHANGELOG.md`.

Use `dbx changelog --dry-run` to preview the proposed root entry without touching
any file; the log line reports the active `target` (or `disabled`).

### Workspace changelogs

Each versioned workspace gets **its own `CHANGELOG.md`** (created if missing),
headed by the version the plan assigned it. A workspace's entry only lists its
**related commits**: those touching the workspace directory **or any workspace it
transitively depends on**, resolved from the project dependency graph
(`.dbx/toolchain/projects.json`, written by `dbx projects`). So a change in a
shared package shows up in the changelog of every package that consumes it, not
just in its own.

Without a graph (eg. `dbx projects` was never run), a workspace falls back to
filtering on its own directory only. A workspace with no related commits is
skipped (no empty entry, no file created).

## CLI

```bash
dbx changelog                       # bump + write (uses the config versioning)
dbx changelog --dry-run             # preview the root entry
dbx changelog --range v1.2.0..HEAD  # scan a specific range
dbx changelog --version 2.0.0       # force a version (retags the changelogs)
dbx changelog --format-only         # regroup existing changelogs, no bump
```

The generated `changelog` workflow runs `dbx changelog --range …` on every push
to the `dev` branches (or `main` when `dev` is unset), so versioning is applied
from CI as well as locally.

## Writing commit messages

The changelog is rendered from commit **subjects and bodies**, so what you commit
is what readers see. Watch out for characters that a **shell** re-interprets —
especially when a message is drafted by an **AI/LLM** and committed through
`git commit -m "…"`.

### Shell escaping

* **PowerShell** treats a backtick as its escape character, so `` `r `` / `` `n `` /
  `` `t `` / `` `b `` become CR / LF / TAB / backspace. A preceding `\` is left
  behind, so `` `resolveVite `` can land in the changelog as a stray `\`, a CR and
  `esolveVite`.
* **bash** runs an unquoted `` `…` `` as command substitution, and `$(…)` / `${…}`
  expand before `git` ever sees them.

The result is invisible control characters, stray `\` and dropped letters. The
toolchain strips the predictable artifacts
(`stripControlChars`/`sanitizeText`) but **cannot restore a character the shell
already consumed**.

### Authoring safely

* Prefer a **file over `-m`**: `git commit -F message.txt`, or a quoted heredoc
  (`git commit -F - <<'EOF' … EOF`) — nothing is re-interpreted. Avoid assembling
  multi-line messages inline in PowerShell.
* When an AI/LLM drafts the message, strip **typographic characters** before
  committing: curly quotes (`’ “ ”`), em/en dashes (`— –`), non-breaking spaces,
  zero-width characters and emoji all survive into the changelog and can break
  `commitlint` or the markdown.
* **Preview the entry**: `dbx changelog --dry-run` prints the proposed entry —
  check it for stray `\`, `\r`, `\b`, `\t` or mojibake before releasing.

## Troubleshooting

### `No "exports" main defined in … conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits`

Seen from the Conventional Commits VS Code extension (`vivaxy.vscode-conventional-commits`),
usually alongside empty type/scope suggestions and a `The cwd is …` line:

```
commitlint: Error: No "exports" main defined in
  node_modules/conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits/package.json
```

This is a **known upstream commitlint bug** (commitlint#4864): the generated
config `extends: ['@commitlint/config-conventional']`, which sets
`parserPreset: 'conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits'`, and v10 of that
package is **ESM-only** (`exports` has no `require`/`default`), so the extension's
bundled (older) commitlint cannot `require.resolve` it. The config is read fine —
the *preset* fails to resolve, so the extension falls back to empty rules.

The husky hook and CI are unaffected when commitlint is recent enough to resolve
pure-ESM presets (commitlint ≥ 21.2.3). If your local commitlint is older, pin
the preset to the last CJS-compatible release:

```json
{
    "resolutions": { "conventional-changelog-conventionalcommits": "9.3.1" }
}
```

(Use `overrides` instead of `resolutions` for npm.) Updating the extension to a
version bundling the fixed commitlint also resolves it.

## Releases

The generated `release` workflow opens a release PR whose body is the
**aggregated changelog**: every entry from the last tag (`git describe --tags --abbrev=0`) up to the latest version, not just the newest one. So a release
that skips versions (eg. `v1.7.0` → `v1.7.8`) still documents `1.7.1`–`1.7.8`
in one place.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/tsconfig.md
---
# tsconfig

The `tsconfig` section generates every workspace's `tsconfig.json` from a
workspace default tsconfig (`tsconfig.default.json`), layering path aliases and
project references from a single root workspaces tsconfig
(`tsconfig.workspaces.json`). It runs only at a **monorepo root**
(`project.type: 'monorepo-root'`); a single project keeps its hand-written
tsconfig untouched.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        project: { type: 'monorepo-root', name: 'acme', scope: '@acme' },
        tsconfig: { aliases: true, refs: true, indent: 4 },
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` regenerates the managed `tsconfig.json` files and tracks them in
`.dbx/toolchain/manifest.json`; `dbx sync --check` is the CI gate. See
[Configuration](/guide/config#opt-in-by-presence) for the opt-in-by-presence
shorthand (`tsconfig: true` enables the defaults).

## Why so many tsconfig files?

TypeScript's language service (IntelliSense, diagnostics, autocomplete, "go to
definition", project references, ...) **always** picks up the file literally
named `tsconfig.json`. It offers no way to point the editor at a different file,
and it only understands the options it can express in a single config.

That single-file constraint is painful in practice:

* **Builds need different options than the editor.** `tsc` for a build wants
  `declaration`/`composite`/`emitDeclarationOnly`, a wider `include` and no
  `noEmit`, while the editor wants fast, no-emit checking of `src`. Cramming both
  into one `tsconfig.json` makes one of the two slower or wrong.
* **A monorepo has many projects with different options.** Each workspace wants
  its own `include`/`lib`/`types`/`jsx`, but the editor only reads the nearest
  `tsconfig.json`.
* **The language service can get slow.** For TypeScript (especially ≤ 7) the
  editor loads and type-checks whatever the `tsconfig.json` includes; a config
  that pulls in every workspace (or the whole build graph) can noticeably slow
  IntelliSense. Keeping the editor config small and correct matters.
* **Hand-managing the graph is tedious.** Path aliases and project references
  have to stay in sync with the workspace list, and a stale reference silently
  degrades the editor.

The toolchain splits the concerns so each file has one job, and `dbx sync`
keeps the generated `tsconfig.json` (the file the LSP actually reads) in sync
with a shared workspaces tsconfig that declares the `paths` + `references`.

**NOTE:** the `paths` + `references` in `tsconfig.workspaces.json` automatically resolves relative paths in each workspace's generated tsconfig.

## The files

The generator reads two hand-authored inputs (`tsconfig.default.json`,
`tsconfig.workspaces.json`) and writes one managed output (`tsconfig.json`):

| File                       | Owner      | Role                                                                              |
| -------------------------- | ---------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tsconfig.base.json`       | you        | Shared compiler options that every workspace config extends.                      |
| `tsconfig.default.json`    | you        | A workspace's own options — the **input** the generator reads. **Optional.**      |
| `tsconfig.build.json`      | you        | Build/emit options (`tsc -p tsconfig.build.json`). **Optional, never rewritten.** |
| `tsconfig.workspaces.json` | you (root) | The root `paths` + `references` the generator expands. **Optional.**              |
| `tsconfig.json`            | generated  | Extends `tsconfig.default.json` + the workspaces aliases/references.              |

Only `tsconfig.json` must keep its name — that is the file TypeScript's LSP
reads. Everything else is optional and, if you prefer, renameable (see
[Renaming the files](#renaming-the-files)):

* **No `tsconfig.default.json`**: there is nothing to expand (the task logs a
  message and, when workspaces are expected, warns — see [Warnings](#warnings)).
* **No `tsconfig.build.json`**: builds simply use another config; it is never
  required or rewritten.
* **No `tsconfig.workspaces.json`**: each workspace still gets a `tsconfig.json`
  that extends its own default, but there are no shared `paths`/`references` to
  wire.

The `{{envTypesFile}}` token in the templates (default `src/env.d.ts`) is
resolved when a project is scaffolded, so a generated config's `include` points
at the project's env types file.

## Options

| Option        | Type                 | Default                    | Description                                                         |
| ------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`     | `boolean`            | enabled when defined       | Master switch (only meaningful with `project.type: monorepo-root`). |
| `aliases`     | `boolean`            | `true`                     | Inject `compilerOptions.paths` from the workspaces config.          |
| `refs`        | `boolean`            | `false`                    | Wire project references between workspaces.                         |
| `composite`   | `boolean`            | `false`                    | Emit `composite: true` on the generated configs.                    |
| `glob`        | `string \| string[]` | `**/tsconfig.default.json` | Glob(s) for the workspace default tsconfig files to expand.         |
| `exclude`     | `string \| string[]` | common ignored paths       | Glob(s) excluded from `glob`.                                       |
| `gitignore`   | `boolean`            | `true`                     | Respect `.gitignore` files (root + nested).                         |
| `defaultFile` | `string`             | `tsconfig.default.json`    | The workspace default tsconfig file name.                           |
| `buildFile`   | `string`             | `tsconfig.build.json`      | The workspace build tsconfig file name.                             |
| `indent`      | `number`             | `4`                        | JSON indentation of the generated files.                            |
| `rootFile`    | `string`             | `tsconfig.workspaces.json` | The workspaces tsconfig file name.                                  |

### `aliases`

When on (the default), each generated `tsconfig.json` gets a
`compilerOptions.paths` block derived from the workspaces tsconfig's `paths`.
The generator rewrites every alias relative to the workspace it is writing, and
**drops** any alias that resolves to the workspace itself (or into its own
subtree) so a package never maps its own import back to a self-reference.

### `refs`

When on, the workspaces `references` are merged with each workspace's own
`references`, deduplicated, rewritten relative to the workspace, and pruned
whenever the target config is not `composite` (a reference to a non-composite
project is invalid). This is what lets `tsc -b` build the graph in order.

### `composite`

When on, the generated configs spread the workspaces tsconfig's
`compilerOptions` (including `composite: true`, `declaration`,
`emitDeclarationOnly`, ...) and merge its `types`. Leave it off unless you build
the graph with `tsc --build`.

### `glob`

The glob(s) selecting the workspace default tsconfig files to expand. A single
string or an array:

```ts
tsconfig: {
    glob: '**/tsconfig.default.json';
}
tsconfig: {
    glob: ['packages/*/tsconfig.default.json', 'apps/*/tsconfig.default.json'];
}
```

It defaults to `**/<defaultFile>`, so setting `defaultFile` alone is usually
enough.

### `exclude` / `gitignore`

`exclude` drops paths from `glob`; it adds to the common ignored paths the
toolchain already skips (`node_modules`, `.dbx`, `dist`, `build`, `coverage`,
`.turbo`, `.git`, `.yarn`, ...). `gitignore` (on by default) additionally honours
the repo's `.gitignore` files — **root and nested**, each scoped to its own
directory, like git — so an ignored workspace is never scanned:

```ts
tsconfig: {
    glob: '**/tsconfig.default.json',
    exclude: ['**/legacy/**'],
    gitignore: true,
}
```

Set `gitignore: false` to scan ignored paths anyway.

### Renaming the files

`defaultFile`, `buildFile` and `rootFile` rename the files the generator reads
and writes:

```ts
tsconfig: {
    defaultFile: 'tsconfig.src.json',       // expanded into tsconfig.json
    buildFile: 'tsconfig.dist.json',        // read, never rewritten
    rootFile: 'tsconfig.graph.json',        // the workspaces paths + references
}
```

Only `tsconfig.json` is fixed (TypeScript's LSP requirement). Project detection
looks for `tsconfig.workspaces.json` / `tsconfig.default.json` by default, but
honours `rootFile` / `defaultFile` when they are set in the config.

### `indent`

The JSON indentation of every generated file (default `4`).

## How generation works

For each workspace matched by `glob`, the generator:

1. reads its default tsconfig and, when present, the workspaces tsconfig;
2. writes a sibling `tsconfig.json` that `extends: './<defaultFile>'`, layering
   the workspaces `compilerOptions` (aliases/types) and `references` on top;
3. leaves `tsconfig.build.json` alone — it is a user-owned input, like the
   default tsconfig.

Because the output only ever `extends` the default and adds the workspaces
wiring, your workspace-specific options stay in the default tsconfig (the file
the generator reads, not the one it writes).

## Warnings

When a sync finds **no** workspace tsconfig files, it warns (in the CLI logs and
as a VS Code notification) if either:

* `refs` or `composite` is enabled, or
* a `tsconfig.workspaces.json` is present,

because in those cases workspaces are clearly expected. Otherwise it logs a
quiet "nothing to do" message.

```
no workspace tsconfig files found (looked for **/tsconfig.default.json), but project references + tsconfig.workspaces.json have nothing to wire.
```

## The workspaces config

`tsconfig.workspaces.json` holds the `paths` and `references` the generator
expands. Scaffold it with `project:init:monorepo`, or build it programmatically
from a workspace list:

```ts
import { buildMonorepoTsconfig, renderMonorepoTsconfig } from '@deltabox/toolchain/tsconfig';

const config = buildMonorepoTsconfig({
    scope: '@acme',
    workspaces: [
        { alias: 'core', dir: 'packages/core' },
        { alias: 'cli', dir: 'packages/cli' },
    ],
});
// -> { compilerOptions: { composite, paths: { '@acme/core': ['./packages/core/src/index.ts'], ... } },
//      references: [{ path: './packages/core/tsconfig.json' }, ...] }
renderMonorepoTsconfig({ scope: '@acme', workspaces: [{ alias: 'core', dir: 'packages/core' }] });
```

## CLI

```bash
dbx tsconfig                       # regenerate every workspace tsconfig.json
dbx tsconfig --no-aliases          # skip the workspaces path aliases
dbx tsconfig --refs                # wire project references
dbx tsconfig --composite           # emit composite: true
dbx tsconfig -i 2                  # JSON indentation
dbx tsconfig --glob "packages/*/tsconfig.default.json" "apps/*/tsconfig.default.json"
dbx tsconfig --exclude "**/legacy/**"     # exclude paths (on top of the defaults)
dbx tsconfig --no-gitignore               # do not respect .gitignore files
dbx tsconfig --default-file tsconfig.src.json
dbx tsconfig --build-file tsconfig.dist.json
dbx tsconfig --root-file tsconfig.workspaces.json
```

Every flag overrides the matching `tsconfig` option; with no flags the command
uses the config defaults. `dbx sync` runs the same generator through the
[tsconfig sync task](#sync--ci).

## Programmatic API

```ts
import {
    generateTsconfigs,
    runTsconfigCli,
    renderTsconfigBase,
    renderTsconfigDefault,
    renderTsconfigBuild,
    renderTsconfigTemplates,
    buildMonorepoTsconfig,
    renderMonorepoTsconfig,
    tsconfigSyncTask,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/tsconfig';
```

| Export                                                                 | Description                                   |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| `generateTsconfigs(options)`                                           | Expand every default tsconfig (dry-run-able). |
| `runTsconfigCli(argv?)`                                                | The `dbx tsconfig` entry point.               |
| `renderTsconfigBase` / `renderTsconfigDefault` / `renderTsconfigBuild` | Render a template with replacements.          |
| `renderTsconfigTemplates(replacements?)`                               | Render every template keyed by file name.     |
| `buildMonorepoTsconfig(options)` / `renderMonorepoTsconfig(options)`   | The workspaces config (object / JSON text).   |
| `tsconfigSyncTask()`                                                   | The sync task wired into `dbx sync`.          |

`generateTsconfigs` returns one result per workspace (with `newTsconfig`,
`originalConfig`, ...); pass `write: false` for a dry run. The task-level
options are documented in the [Programmatic API](/guide/api#deltaboxtoolchaintsconfig)
reference.

## Sync & CI

At a monorepo root with the section enabled, `dbx sync` runs the tsconfig task
and reports the regenerated files:

```
tsconfig: regenerated 6 workspace tsconfig(s).
```

The task watches `tsconfig.workspaces.json` and every default tsconfig, keeps
`tsconfig.build.json`, and only applies to `monorepo-root` projects. Run
`dbx sync --check` in CI to fail when a generated `tsconfig.json` drifts from
its inputs.

## Per-project configs

A non-root `dbx.config.*` is **merged over** the nearest ancestor
`dbx.config.*`: nested options are combined, and leaf options (booleans,
strings, numbers, arrays) in the project override the root. So a workspace can
tweak just its own `tsconfig` (or any other section) and inherit the rest. See
[Configuration → Nested configs](/guide/config#nested-configs) for the rules.

## Scaffolding

`dbx project:init:monorepo` writes `tsconfig.base.json` + a `tsconfig.workspaces.json`;
`dbx project:init:workspace` writes the workspace's `tsconfig.default.json` /
`tsconfig.build.json` / `tsconfig.json` (and a `dbx.config.ts`). See the
[Monorepo Guide](/guide/monorepo#tsconfig-generation) for the full flow.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/biome.md
---
# Biome

The `biome` section generates a `biome.json` for consumers that still want a
Biome config. The toolchain itself is built on **Oxc** (Oxfmt + Oxlint) through
Vite+, but a repo that runs Biome directly can let the toolchain manage its
`biome.json` from the same `dbx.config.*`.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        biome: true, // or { overrides: { ... } }
    },
});
```

`dbx sync` writes `biome.json`, resolving the `{{name}}` / `{{scope}}`
replacement tokens and merging your overrides over the defaults.

## Options

| Option      | Type                      | Default              | Description                                  |
| ----------- | ------------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`   | `boolean`                 | enabled when defined | Master switch.                               |
| `vscode`    | `boolean`                 | `true`               | Write the Biome VS Code settings/extensions. |
| `overrides` | `Record<string, unknown>` | —                    | Deep-merged over the generated `biome.json`. |

### `overrides`

Overrides are merged into the generated config **recursively**, and **arrays are
unioned** (not replaced) — so `files.includes` can be extended:

```ts
biome: {
    overrides: {
        files: { includes: ['!**/generated/**'] },
        formatter: { indentWidth: 2 },
    },
}
```

### `vscode`

When on (the default), the sync also writes the recommended Biome VS Code
settings and the Biome extension recommendation (see
[VS Code Extension](/guide/vscode)). Set `biome: { vscode: false }` to skip them.

## Programmatic API

```ts
import {
    biomeConfig,
    biomeSyncTask,
    biomeVscodeSettings,
    mergeBiomeConfig,
    renderBiomeConfig,
    renderBiomeJson,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/biome';
```

| Export                                  | Description                                              |
| --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `biomeSyncTask()`                       | The sync task (writes `biome.json`).                     |
| `biomeConfig` / `biomeVscodeSettings`   | The generic Biome config / recommended VS Code settings. |
| `renderBiomeConfig(tokens, overrides?)` | Resolve tokens + merge overrides into an object.         |
| `renderBiomeJson(tokens, overrides?)`   | Serialize the rendered config.                           |
| `mergeBiomeConfig(base, patch)`         | The recursive/array-union merge used above.              |

> Migrating **from** Biome to Oxc is a different concern — see
> [Migrations](/guide/migrations).

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/vite.md
---
# Vite+

The `vite` section holds the **entire Vite+ configuration**. Every key is passed
through verbatim to Vite+, so `dbx.config.*` stays the only hand-authored root
config; `dbx sync` writes a thin root `vite.config.ts` that resolves it at load
time.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        vite: {
            fmt: { semi: true, singleQuote: true },
            lint: { ignorePatterns: ['dist/**'] },
            test: { include: ['src/**/*.test.ts'], environment: 'node' },
            run: { tasks: { build: { command: 'tsdown --config-loader unrun' } } },
        },
    },
});
```

The section is typed as Vite+'s own config (`ToolchainViteConfig` = Vite's
`UserConfig` as augmented by Vite+), so the whole Vite+ surface autocompletes in
`dbx.config.ts`.

## The generated shim

`dbx sync` writes a fixed `vite.config.ts`:

```ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';

// Generated by @deltabox/toolchain — edit the vite section in dbx.config and run `dbx sync`.
import { resolveVite } from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';

export default defineConfig(resolveVite({ cwd: import.meta.dirname }));
```

`resolveVite(options?)` resolves the **same-directory** `dbx.config.*` (so a
nested workspace `vite.config.ts` uses its own config), or the `toolchain` you
pass, then returns `toolchain.vite`. The file never drifts, because the real
config stays in `dbx.config.*`.

The root shim must live at the **root**: `vp run`, `vp check` and `vp staged` do
not accept `--config`, so the shim has to be the file Vite+ loads.

## Options

| Option   | Type      | Default | Description                              |
| -------- | --------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| `config` | `boolean` | `true`  | Write the managed `vite.config.ts` shim. |

Everything else under `vite` is Vite+ config (plugins, `test`, `lint`, `fmt`,
`run.tasks`, ...). Set `vite: { config: false }` to leave a hand-written
`vite.config.ts` alone (the section is still read for provider colouring and the
`dbx` provider passthrough).

## Keep the shim out of Oxfmt

Add `/vite.config.ts` to `vite.fmt.ignorePatterns`, otherwise `vp fmt` rewrites
the generated shim and `dbx sync --check` reports drift:

```ts
vite: {
    fmt: {
        ignorePatterns: ['/vite.config.ts'];
    }
}
```

`dbx migrate --from vite` adds it for you (see
[Migrations](/guide/migrations#vite-config)).

## Commands

Vite+ commands are reachable directly or through the `vite` namespace, and are
registered as a provider (see [Providers](/guide/providers)):

```bash
dbx fmt                 # a bare Vite+ command forwards to `vp fmt`
dbx run -r build        # forwards to `vp run -r build`
dbx vite dev            # explicit namespace (always works)
dbx vite:build          # named alias for `vp build`
```

A bare `dbx <command>` is forwarded to Vite+ when the name (or a Vite+ alias)
matches — built-in commands win, so `dbx migrate` stays the toolchain's
migration.

## Programmatic API

```ts
import {
    resolveVite,
    renderViteConfig,
    viteConfigObject,
    viteProvider,
    viteSyncTask,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';
```

| Export                      | Description                                                               |
| --------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `resolveVite(options?)`     | Resolve `toolchain.vite` from a `dbx.config.*` (or a passed `toolchain`). |
| `renderViteConfig()`        | The managed `vite.config.ts` shim source.                                 |
| `viteConfigObject(config?)` | The `vite` section without the toolchain opt-out `config`.                |
| `viteSyncTask()`            | The sync task (writes the shim).                                          |
| `viteProvider()`            | The Vite+ provider descriptor.                                            |

See [Configuration](/guide/config#vite) for the `dbx.config` integration and the
[Providers](/guide/providers) guide for the passthrough commands.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/watch.md
---
# Watch

The `watch` section configures `dbx watch`, which syncs once and then re-runs on
input changes.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        watch: { enabled: true, debounce: 150 },
    },
});
```

## Options

| Option      | Type                 | Default              | Description                                 |
| ----------- | -------------------- | -------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
| `enabled`   | `boolean`            | enabled when defined | Watch by default.                           |
| `debounce`  | `number`             | `150`                | Debounce window in ms before a re-sync.     |
| `exclude`   | `string \| string[]` | common ignored paths | Glob(s) excluded from watching.             |
| `gitignore` | `boolean`            | `true`               | Respect `.gitignore` files (root + nested). |

`exclude` adds to the common ignored paths (`node_modules`, `.dbx`, `dist`,
`build`, ...), and `gitignore` also honours the repo's `.gitignore` files (root
and nested, each scoped to its own directory) so ignored directories are never
watched. Set `gitignore: false` to watch them anyway.

```ts
watch: { exclude: ['**/fixtures/**'], gitignore: true }
```

## How it works

```bash
dbx watch
```

`dbx watch` runs one sync, then watches the config file plus every task's
`watch` globs and re-runs on change. Writes made by the sync itself must not
re-trigger a run, so a short quiet window follows each sync.

Only **input** files are watched (eg. `dbx.config.*`, `tsconfig.default.json`,
`tsconfig.workspaces.json`), never the generated outputs — so a sync can never
loop on its own writes.

`dbx watch --force` runs even when there is no `dbx.config.*`, and
`watch: { enabled: false }` disables it (so a plain `dbx watch` warns and exits).

## VS Code

The VS Code extension has its own debounced scheduler that mirrors this
behaviour (see [VS Code Extension](/guide/vscode#auto-sync)); the `watch` section
configures the **CLI** `dbx watch` command.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/logger.md
---
# Logger

Every toolchain message goes through one logger, so output stays consistent and
respects a single configuration. The `logger` section controls its level,
colours and prefix.

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        logger: { level: 'debug', color: false, name: 'dbx' },
    },
});
```

## Options

| Option  | Type                                               | Default | Description                    |
| ------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------ |
| `level` | `debug` | `info` | `warn` | `error` | `silent` | `info`  | Minimum level to print.        |
| `color` | `boolean`                                          | `true`  | Force colours on/off.          |
| `name`  | `string`                                           | `dbx`   | Prefix for non-indented lines. |

Colour is **on by default** (the toolchain forces it rather than relying on TTY
autodetection); `--no-color` or `logger: { color: false }` turn it off. Human
output is rendered with [`@clack/prompts`](https://bombshell.dev/clack) — level
symbols (`•` info, `◆` success, `▲` warn, `■` error) and a guide.

## CLI overrides

| Flag                | Description                                                |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `--log-level <lvl>` | Minimum level: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`, `silent`. |
| `--color`           | Force coloured output (the default).                       |
| `--no-color`        | Disable coloured output.                                   |

They win over the config and may appear before or after the subcommand.

## Machine output

`--json` (and provider passthroughs) write raw, unprefixed, undecorated output
through the same logger (`logger.raw`), so it is safe to pipe into `jq` or
another tool.

## Providers

Provider passthrough commands (Vite+) follow the logger's colour setting, and the
[`providers`](/guide/providers#colour) section can force provider colours on or
off independently. `color: false` runs the wrapped binary with `NO_COLOR=1` and
`FORCE_COLOR=0`.

## Programmatic API

```ts
import {
    configureLogger,
    createLogger,
    getLogger,
    isLogLevel,
    logger,
    normalizeLogLevel,
    setLogConfig,
    setLogOverrides,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/shared';
```

| Export                             | Description                                            |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ |
| `logger`                           | The active logger (delegates to the current instance). |
| `createLogger(options?)`           | Build a logger with explicit options.                  |
| `setLogConfig(section)`            | Apply the `logger` config section.                     |
| `setLogOverrides(options)`         | Apply CLI overrides (win over the config).             |
| `configureLogger(options?)`        | Alias for `setLogOverrides`.                           |
| `isLogLevel` / `normalizeLogLevel` | Validate/coerce a level.                               |

Use `logger.info` for human messages and `logger.raw` for machine output; avoid
`console.log` so output stays consistent and respects the config and CLI flags.

---

---
url: https://toolchain.deltabox.studio/guide/providers.md
---
# Providers

A **provider** is an external toolchain exposed through `dbx`: its CLI,
the programmatic API and the VS Code extension. Providers contribute namespaced
commands and a descriptor the editor reads over `dbx providers --json`.

## List providers

```bash
dbx providers          # table
dbx providers --json   # descriptor (id, binary, commands, actions)
```

## Vite+ (`vite-plus`)

The bundled provider wraps the `vp` binary — the unified Vite / Vitest / Oxlint /
Oxfmt / Rolldown / tsdown toolchain.

### Resolution

`dbx vite:*` resolves `vp` in this order:

1. the project-local shim (`node_modules/.bin/vp`),
2. a global `vp` on `PATH`,
3. `npx --yes vite-plus`.

### Generic passthrough

```bash
dbx vite dev
dbx vite build
dbx vite add zod
dbx vite check
```

Everything after `vite` is forwarded verbatim to `vp`, so all Vite+ commands and
flags are reachable. A bare `dbx <command>` whose name is a Vite+ command (or a
Vite+ alias) is forwarded too, so `dbx fmt` / `dbx run -r build` need no `vite`
namespace — built-in commands win (`dbx migrate` stays the toolchain's).

### Colour

Provider output keeps `vp`'s own colours, but follows the logger's colour state.
The global `--no-color` flag turns provider colour off, and the `providers`
section can opt out on its own even on a colour terminal:

```ts
export default defineConfig({
    toolchain: {
        providers: { color: false },
    },
});
```

When colour is off, `dbx` runs `vp` with `NO_COLOR=1` and `FORCE_COLOR=0` so the
wrapped process emits plain output. Leave the section unset to let `vp` detect
colour from its own terminal.

### Named commands

Every catalogued subcommand is also available as a first-class command for
discovery + the editor:

```
vite:create  vite:migrate  vite:dev  vite:check  vite:lint  vite:fmt  vite:test
vite:build   vite:pack     vite:run  vite:add    vite:remove vite:update ...
vite:toolchain vite:upgrade vite:implode
```

### Programmatic

```ts
import {
    resolveVp,
    runVp,
    hasVp,
    vpVersion,
    describeVp,
    resolveVpCommand,
    viteCommandName,
    VP_COMMANDS,
} from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';

if (hasVp(process.cwd())) {
    await runVp(['check'], { cwd: process.cwd() });
}
```

| Export                                 | Description                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `resolveVp(cwd?)`                      | Resolve the `vp` invocation (`{ exe, args, source }`).                      |
| `hasVp(cwd?)`                          | Whether a local/global `vp` is available (no `npx` fallback).               |
| `runVp(args, options?)`                | Run `vp`, streaming output or `mode: 'capture'`; never exits the host.      |
| `vpVersion(cwd?)` / `describeVp(cwd?)` | The `vp --version` output / a one-line resolution description.              |
| `which(bin)`                           | Find an executable on `PATH` (resolves `PATHEXT` on Windows).               |
| `resolveVpCommand(name)`               | Resolve a subcommand **or alias** to its canonical name (`i` -> `install`). |
| `viteCommandName(name)`                | The `dbx` command name for a `vp` subcommand (`dev` -> `vite:dev`).         |
| `VP_COMMANDS`                          | The `vp` command catalog that drives the CLI + the provider descriptor.     |

```ts
// A bare `dbx <command>` falls through to `vite` when it names a Vite+ command.
resolveVpCommand('fmt'); // 'fmt'
viteCommandName('fmt'); // 'vite:fmt'
```

### Use dbx from Vite+

Vite+ consumers can drive dbx from `vite.config.ts`, so a Vite+-only project
still gets dbx's generated/managed files:

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite-plus';

import { dbx, DBX_TASKS } from '@deltabox/toolchain/vite';

export default defineConfig({
    plugins: [dbx()],
    run: { tasks: { ...DBX_TASKS } },
    // your usual Vite / Vite+ config
});
```

* The `dbx()` plugin runs `dbx sync` before the dev server / build, or
  `dbx sync --check` in CI (which fails the build when generated files are out of
  date), and re-syncs when a `dbx.config.*` / `tsconfig.*.json` input changes.
* The plugin resolves the `dbx` binary from the project first: the local
  `node_modules/.bin/dbx`, then the project's own `@deltabox/toolchain` bin. A
  global `dbx` on `PATH` is used **only when the project doesn't pin the
  toolchain at all** — otherwise it's skipped (with a warning) in favour of
  `npx @deltabox/toolchain@<pinned>`. That way a stale global install can never
  run and silently revert the project's generated files.
* `run: { tasks: { ...DBX_TASKS } }` also exposes `vp run dbx:sync` /
  `vp run dbx:check`. Vite+ reads `run.tasks` from the **static** config (a
  plugin's `config` hook is ignored), so the tasks are spread in the config
  rather than added by the plugin. Drop the `run` block if you don't want them.
* Because Vite Task runs a task's `command` through a shell, `DBX_TASKS` bakes in
  the binary resolved by `resolveDbx` (the project's own, or the pinned `npx`
  fallback) rather than relying on `dbx` being on `PATH` — a missing environment
  then warns instead of silently running the wrong binary. Use `dbxTaskCommand(sub)`
  to build a task command for another subcommand.

## Custom providers

Register extra providers in `.dbx/toolchain/providers.json` (a list of provider
descriptors). `toolchainProviders()` merges them with the built-ins, so a custom
provider's commands become `dbx` commands — `dbx <command.name>` forwards to
`<binary> <subcommand> ...` — and it shows up in `dbx providers` and the editor.

```json
[
    {
        "id": "echo",
        "name": "Echo",
        "binary": "node",
```
